headline: Hidden 390-Million-Year-Old Crater Found Thanks to Curious Camper
meta_description: Amateur astronomer Joël Lapointe spotted a mysterious circular feature on satellite maps while planning a Quebec camping trip, leading to the confirmation of a…
summary_short: An amateur astronomer planning a camping trip in Quebec accidentally discovered evidence of a 25-kilometer-wide impact crater that formed 390 million years ago.
body:
An amateur astronomer searching satellite maps for a camping spot in Quebec's remote Côte-Nord region accidentally made a discovery that would captivate planetary scientists: a massive impact crater hidden in plain sight. In 2024, Joël Lapointe noticed a strange circular depression near Lake Marsal and suspected it might be the mark of an ancient collision. His intuition proved correct. After researchers confirmed the site through field expeditions in October 2025, the 25-kilometer-wide structure was identified as Uhackatik—the largest impact crater discovered since 2018—formed roughly 390 million years ago. If such an impact occurred today, it would cause regional devastation on a scale that would wipe out major cities and trigger global climate impacts.

Getting to the site tested the resolve of planetary geologist Gordon Osinski and his team. A floatplane could not reach the shore, forcing the researchers to wade through 50 meters of water before reaching land. The landscape that awaited them was unforgiving: swampy terrain thick with insects and what Osinski described as "deep, twisty, gnarly vegetation." Yet the difficulty paid off. Within days, the team discovered shatter cones—distinctive rock formations created only under the extreme pressures of an impact—providing undeniable evidence that this was no volcano but a genuine impact crater.

Lapointe's discovery embodies the power of citizen observation. "I encourage everyone to not ignore intuition or an observation, even if it isn't part of your field of expertise," he reflected. His simple curiosity while planning a getaway has added to humanity's understanding of Earth's collision history and reminds us that major scientific breakthroughs sometimes come from the most unexpected places.
quick_facts: Amateur astronomer Joël Lapointe spotted the crater on satellite maps in 2024
25-kilometer-wide impact crater formed 390 million years ago in Quebec
Researchers waded 50 meters through water to reach the remote site
Shatter cones provided definitive proof of impact, not volcanic origin
Largest crater discovered since Hiawatha in 2018
